definition: A relational database from Oracle Corporation. Its SQL traditionally uses MINUS for set difference; Oracle 21c documentation also lists EXCEPT.
Microsoft's commercial relational database. Its SQL dialect is called T-SQL and includes a PIVOT operator.
A cloud data-warehouse service for analytics queries over large data sets. Its SQL includes a QUALIFY clause for filtering on window function results.
Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse, queried with SQL. Like Snowflake and DuckDB, it supports QUALIFY.
An in-process analytical database, often described as "SQLite for analytics": it runs inside your program and is built for fast aggregate queries over columns.
Data build tool: a framework for writing analytics transformations as SELECT statements (models), usually chains of CTEs, which it runs in a data warehouse in dependency order.
A Python library for working with tables of data (DataFrames). Its pivot_table function reshapes long rows into a pivot with one column per category.
example: df.pivot_table(index="month", columns="category", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")

definition: Business intelligence tool: software such as Tableau, Power BI or Looker that queries a database and presents charts, dashboards and pivot tables to business users.

The international standard (ISO/IEC 9075) that defines the SQL language. Databases follow it to different degrees and add their own extensions, which is why the same query can behave differently in PostgreSQL and SQLite.
An add-on package that adds functions, types or operators to a PostgreSQL database, installed with CREATE EXTENSION. tablefunc, which provides crosstab(), is one.
example: CREATE EXTENSION tablefunc; makes crosstab() available in that database.

definition: An option of FETCH FIRST n ROWS (PostgreSQL 13+) that also returns any further rows tied with the last row kept, according to the ORDER BY. It answers "top N, including ties at the cut-off".
example: FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES on totals 200, 120, 90, 60, 60, ... returns 5 rows.

definition: A clause that writes rows out literally, such as VALUES (1, 5), (2, 7). It supplies rows to INSERT, and in PostgreSQL it can also be used like a small table in FROM or USING.
The || operator, which joins two strings end to end. In PostgreSQL it returns the text type, and it also merges jsonb values.
example: 'Mia' || ' > ' || 'Raj' gives 'Mia > Raj'.

definition: The type of a true/false value. In SQL a boolean expression can be TRUE, FALSE or, because of NULL, UNKNOWN. PostgreSQL has a real boolean type; SQLite stores TRUE and FALSE as the integers 1 and 0.
example: In SQLite SUM(x > 1) counts matching rows; PostgreSQL rejects SUM of a boolean.

definition: The comparison set operations, DISTINCT and GROUP BY use to recognise duplicate values, treating two NULLs as the same. PostgreSQL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM provides null-safe equality for individual values. SQLite also spells this IS, but both spellings have special truth-testing rules when TRUE or FALSE is the right-hand literal.
example: NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, but NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL is TRUE.

definition: A join that keeps each left-hand row at most once if at least one matching right-hand row exists, without adding the right-hand columns. IN (subquery) and EXISTS express semi-joins.
example: Ana has three orders but appears once in WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders).

definition: A keyword allowing a FROM subquery to refer to columns from earlier FROM items. Its result is defined for each relevant outer row, although the optimiser chooses the physical execution strategy; PostgreSQL supports it and SQLite does not.
example: CROSS JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE r.category = c.category LIMIT 2) gets the top two per category.

definition: A subquery that returns at most one row of one column, so it can be used wherever a single value can. Zero rows gives NULL; more than one row is an error in PostgreSQL.
example: (SELECT AVG(total) FROM orders) is a scalar subquery giving 81.25.

definition: A subquery that does not reference the outer query. The database may compute its result once and reuse it, but the language does not generally guarantee a particular number of physical evaluations, especially for volatile expressions.
A subquery in the FROM clause, which the outer query treats like a temporary table. PostgreSQL before version 16 required it to have an alias.
example: FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY c.id) AS per_cust

definition: An optimiser rewrite that removes a subquery’s dependency on an outer row, often by expressing it as an equivalent join. It permits different execution strategies while preserving NULL and duplicate semantics; it does not guarantee a single physical pass.

A comparison with values returned by a subquery. ANY is true if at least one comparison is true, while ALL is true if every comparison is true; NULL and empty inputs have defined special rules. PostgreSQL supports these forms and SQLite does not.
example: total > ALL (Ana's totals 120, 60, 60) is TRUE only for 200.

definition: A SQL keyword with context-dependent uses. In a quantified comparison, ALL requires the comparison to hold for every subquery value and accepts an empty input; in set operations, an ALL variant preserves multiplicity using that operator’s copy-count rule.
example: UNION ALL of two 4-row results returns 8 rows; UNION returns the distinct ones.

definition: Several values written together in brackets, such as (id, city), and compared as one unit. Both SQLite and PostgreSQL accept them in comparisons and IN.
example: WHERE (id, city) IN (SELECT ...)

definition: A statement about every member of an empty set is true, because there is no member that could break it. This is why x > ALL (empty set) is TRUE and "bought every required item" holds when nothing is required.

A PostgreSQL aggregate whose result depends on the order of its input, given with WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...). percentile_cont and mode are examples. Hypothetical-set aggregates such as rank(value) are a related kind.
example: percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total) gives the median.

definition: PostgreSQL ordered-set aggregates for percentiles. percentile_cont(f) interpolates between neighbouring values, so it can return a value not in the data; percentile_disc(f) returns an actual value from the data. Both ignore NULLs.
example: percentile_cont(0.5) of 10 and 20 is 15; percentile_disc(0.5) is 10.

definition: An optional SQLite extension providing the aggregate functions median(), percentile(), percentile_cont() and percentile_disc(). The sqlite3 command-line tool has included these functions since version 3.47.0. In the SQLite library they have been built into the amalgamation since 3.51.0 but stay off unless SQLite is compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_PERCENTILE (earlier versions shipped them as a separately compiled loadable extension), so an application's SQLite library may not have them.
example: In the sqlite3 command-line tool, or a library build with the extension enabled, median(total) over the totals 30, 45, 45, 60, 60, 90, 120 and 200 returns 60.0.

definition: Estimating a value between two known values, usually along a straight line between them.
example: Halfway between 60 and 90 by linear interpolation is 75.

definition: The keyword that closes a CASE expression: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END. Writing ELSE 0 before END makes unmatched rows contribute 0 instead of NULL, which matters inside SUM.
example: SUM(CASE WHEN feb THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) gives 0, not NULL, for a customer with no February orders.

definition: An operation that combines two sets, such as union, intersection or difference. In SQL, UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine the results of two queries end to end; both sides need the same number of columns with compatible types, matched by position. SQLite calls such a query a compound select.

The SQL set operator keeping rows found in both query results. PostgreSQL gives it higher precedence than UNION and EXCEPT; SQLite uses left-to-right grouping. PostgreSQL INTERSECT ALL keeps the smaller of the two copy counts, while SQLite has no INTERSECT ALL.
example: January INTERSECT March gives Kettle, Mug and Rug.

definition: The SQL set operator keeping rows found in the left query but absent from the right. PostgreSQL EXCEPT ALL subtracts the right copy count from the left, stopping at zero; SQLite supports only the duplicate-removing form. Oracle traditionally spells set difference MINUS.
example: January EXCEPT March gives Toaster; March EXCEPT January gives Lamp.

definition: The items in exactly one of two sets, not both: (A EXCEPT B) UNION (B EXCEPT A).
example: For January and March products it is Toaster and Lamp.

definition: A collection like a set but allowing repeated items, so it records how many copies of each it holds. SQL tables and results are multisets unless duplicates are removed.
example: {1, 1, 2} is a multiset with two copies of 1.

definition: Removing repeated items or rows according to a chosen identity or equality rule. SQL DISTINCT can use sorting, hashing or already ordered input; a loader may instead combine repeated keys before an upsert.

SQLite normally associates a storage class with each value rather than enforcing one rigid type for an entire column. Column affinity still influences conversion, and STRICT tables impose additional type restrictions.
example: SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'y' works in SQLite but fails in PostgreSQL.

definition: The reverse of a pivot: turning several columns of one row into several rows, one per column, giving long (narrow) data.
example: One order row with total and customer_id becomes two rows: (101, total, 120) and (101, cust, 1).

definition: A clause in SQL Server and Oracle that rotates rows into columns. Like conditional aggregation it still needs the output columns listed.
A function from PostgreSQL's tablefunc extension that produces pivot tables. You still declare the output column names and types when calling it.
A GROUP BY option that adds subtotal rows: ROLLUP (a, b) groups by (a, b), then (a), then () for a grand total. Rolled-up columns show NULL. PostgreSQL has it; SQLite does not.
example: GROUP BY ROLLUP (city) gives one row per city plus a total row with city NULL.

definition: A GROUP BY option computing every subset of its listed grouping expressions, including the empty set for a grand total. Two listed expressions therefore generate four grouping sets; every additional expression doubles that count.
A GROUP BY option that lists exactly which groupings to compute in one query; ROLLUP and CUBE are shorthands for common lists.
example: GROUPING SETS ((city), ()) gives per-city rows plus a grand total.

definition: A PostgreSQL function identifying columns omitted from the current grouping set. With one argument it returns zero when the expression participates and one when it was omitted; with several arguments it returns a bit mask, distinguishing subtotal placeholders from real NULL values.
example: GROUPING(c.city) is 1 on the grand-total row.

definition: The keyword that starts a query with one or more common table expressions (CTEs): WITH name AS (subquery) names an intermediate result that the main query, and later CTEs, can read like a table.
example: WITH spend AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT * FROM spend;

definition: A CTE that refers to itself, written WITH RECURSIVE. It is an anchor member plus a recursive term joined by UNION ALL or UNION, and repeats until a pass adds no rows. It walks trees and graphs of unknown depth.
example: Starting from Mia and joining staff on manager_id, it finds the whole org chart.

definition: The first part of a recursive CTE: an ordinary query, run once, that produces the starting rows. It must not refer to the CTE itself.
example: SELECT ... FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL starts the org chart at Mia.

definition: The second part of a recursive CTE, which refers to the CTE's own name. Each pass runs it against only the rows the previous pass produced.

In PostgreSQL’s recursive-CTE algorithm, the current batch of rows supplied to the next recursive step. New rows replace that batch, and recursion stops when it is empty; SQLite describes evaluation as a row queue rather than the same batching algorithm.
The condition that eventually stops a loop or recursion. In a recursive CTE it is usually a WHERE in the recursive term, or a join that runs out of matches.
example: WHERE i < 5 stops the counting CTE after the value 5.

aliases: CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path
definition: PostgreSQL 14+ recursive-CTE syntax that tracks selected identity columns along a path. CYCLE emits the first repeated identity with a cycle marker and prevents following that path further; other paths may still reach the same node.
A guard such as WHERE c.depth < 20 that stops recursion after a fixed number of levels, even if the data contains a cycle.
Data where each row points to a parent row in the same table, forming a tree, such as staff and their managers. Recursive CTEs query it without knowing the depth in advance.

Substituting a CTE's query into the outer query, as if it were written there as a subquery, so the optimiser can push filters into it and use indexes. PostgreSQL 12+ inlines an eligible CTE referenced once.

Keeping an intermediate query result in temporary storage so later operations can read it again. A SELECT CTE may be filled only as far as consumers demand; PostgreSQL MATERIALIZED prevents folding, while SQLite’s materialisation annotations are planner hints.
example: WITH o AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders) prevents an outer id filter from restricting the orders scan; a consumer LIMIT may still stop the CTE early.

definition: A boundary the query planner will not optimise across, such as a materialised CTE: outer filters cannot be pushed inside it. Before PostgreSQL 12, SELECT CTEs were not folded into their parent queries.
An optimisation that moves a filter from an outer query into an inner one, so rows are discarded early and indexes can be used.
example: Inlining lets id = 104 be pushed into the scan of orders.

definition: A PostgreSQL CTE whose body changes rows with INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, or MERGE in versions that support it there. It executes to completion and communicates its changed rows through RETURNING; sibling sub-statements share a snapshot. SQLite does not permit these CTE bodies.
example: WITH moved AS (DELETE ... RETURNING *) INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;

definition: An observable change beyond a returned value, such as modifying rows or advancing a sequence. Such effects and volatile functions constrain optimiser rewrites because changing how often they occur can change behaviour.
A PostgreSQL set-returning function that produces a series of numbers or timestamps, such as every month between two dates. SQLite builds may include it only as an optional extension.
example: generate_series(date '2026-01-01', date '2026-04-01', interval '1 month') gives four dates.

definition: A function that returns rows rather than one value, so it can be used in FROM like a table. json_each, jsonb_array_elements_text and generate_series are examples.
The clause that makes a function a window function and defines its window: PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and a frame. An empty OVER () means the whole result set is one window.
The part of OVER (...) that splits rows into independent groups (partitions) for a window function, like GROUP BY but without collapsing rows. With no PARTITION BY, the whole result is one partition.
example: PARTITION BY customer_id restarts a running total for each customer.

definition: The subset of a partition, relative to the current row, that an aggregate window function sees. With ORDER BY and no frame clause the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
example: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a three-row moving window.

definition: How a window frame’s boundaries are measured. ROWS uses row positions, RANGE uses ordering values, and GROUPS uses groups of equal ordering values; peer-sensitive boundaries and explicit exclusions determine the final contents.
example: With the unbounded-preceding to current-row frame on totals 45 and 45, RANGE gives both the same running sum; ROWS steps through them separately.

definition: The words that set where a window frame starts and ends: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING (the partition's first row), n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING and UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING (the partition's last row).
example: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING covers the whole partition.

definition: Rows in a window partition that have equal values in the window's ORDER BY. In RANGE mode, CURRENT ROW includes all of the current row's peers.
example: Orders 103 and 107 (both 60) are peers under ORDER BY total.

definition: Rows equal on the relevant sort expressions. A unique secondary ordering key makes their order deterministic; including it in a ranking window also changes which rows count as peers.
example: Totals 60 and 60 are tied; ORDER BY total DESC, id puts 103 before 107.

definition: A clause that names a window definition, WINDOW w AS (...), so several window functions can share it with OVER w. SQLite and PostgreSQL both support it.
A window function that numbers rows 1, 2, 3, ... in the window order, giving tied rows different numbers in an arbitrary order unless the ORDER BY breaks the tie.
example: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on DESC) = 1 marks each customer's latest order.

definition: A window function giving tied rows the same rank and then leaving a gap, like a sports table: 4, 4, then 6. It equals 1 plus the number of rows that sort strictly before the row.
example: Totals 60, 60, 45 ranked descending after three larger ones get 4, 4, 6.

definition: A window function giving tied rows the same rank with no gap afterwards: 4, 4, then 5. It equals 1 plus the number of distinct values that sort before the row, which makes it the ranking for "Nth highest distinct value".
A window function that splits a partition's rows into k numbered buckets as equally as possible, with the larger buckets first. It works on positions, so tied values can land in different buckets.
example: NTILE(3) over 8 rows gives bucket sizes 3, 3 and 2.

definition: Strictly, the three cut points that divide a sorted list into four equal parts; the word is also used for the four groups themselves (bottom quarter, second quarter and so on). NTILE(4) assigns rows to those four groups by position.
A window function measuring relative rank: subtract one from RANK and divide by one fewer than the partition’s row count. A one-row partition returns zero; peers receive the same value.

Window functions that read a value from another row: LAG(x) from the previous row in window order, LEAD(x) from the next. Optional arguments give an offset (LAG(x, 12)) and a default to use instead of NULL when there is no such row.
example: LAG(rev) gives February the value 165 from January.

definition: Window functions returning a value from the first or last row of the window frame. With ORDER BY and the default frame, which ends at the current row and its peers, LAST_VALUE usually returns the current row's own value.
A clause in Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB that filters on window function results in the same query, much as HAVING filters on aggregates. PostgreSQL and SQLite do not have it.
example: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1

definition: A cumulative sum in a chosen order. A ROWS frame steps by individual rows, while an ordered default RANGE frame also includes all rows tied with the current one; use an explicit ordering and frame for the intended meaning.
example: Order totals 120, 60, 60 have running totals 120, 180, 240.

definition: An average updated as observations arrive, using a moving window or weights that give recent observations more influence. A SQL AVG window can use row or value-based boundaries; it ignores NULLs and its first frames can be partial.
example: The three-order moving average of 120, 45, 60 is 75.

definition: A PostgreSQL 15+ optimisation: when a query filters on a monotonic window function (for example rn <= 3), the executor stops computing it for a partition once the condition can no longer become true.

The classic query pattern of returning the N best rows within each group, such as each customer's latest order. Usual solutions are ROW_NUMBER in a subquery, DISTINCT ON (for N = 1), or LATERAL with LIMIT.

The query pattern "find the X related to all of a given set of Y", such as customers who bought every listed product. In SQL it is usually filter, group, and compare COUNT(DISTINCT ...) with the size of the set, or a double NOT EXISTS.

The problem of finding runs of consecutive values (islands) separated by missing values (gaps), such as login streaks. A common solution groups by value minus ROW_NUMBER, which is constant within each run.
example: Login days 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9 form islands 1–3, 5–6 and 9.

definition: The fixed shop data used in Advanced SQL: five customers, six products, eight orders and thirteen order lines. It differs from the introductory SQL module’s original shop, so each worked query uses the data stated in its unit.

A technique for reading only the distinct leading values of an index by jumping from one value to the next, instead of reading every entry. PostgreSQL has no built-in loose index scan for queries such as SELECT DISTINCT, but a recursive CTE can emulate it. PostgreSQL 18's B-tree skip scan uses a similar jump for filters on later index columns.
SQLite's storage class for floating-point numbers, stored as 8-byte IEEE floats. A JSON number with a fraction extracted by ->> comes back as REAL.
The rules PostgreSQL uses to pick one result type when values of different types meet, as in the branches of a UNION. If no common type exists, the query fails.
example: SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'y' fails because 'y' cannot become an integer.

definition: PostgreSQL's name for the extra parameter on a type, such as the 10 in varchar(10). Two types that differ only in typmod still count as different in a recursive CTE.

An ordering that compares sequences element by element until a difference is found; under C text collation a shorter equal prefix comes first. SQL text comparisons depend on their collation, so this is not a universal description of every language-aware ordering.

aliases: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
definition: The error raised when an insert or update would create a second row with the same value in a UNIQUE or primary-key column.
A PostgreSQL constraint that forbids any two rows from satisfying a given comparison, such as overlapping time ranges. UNIQUE is the special case of equality.

A function the database runs automatically when a specified event happens on a table, such as before or after a DELETE. In SQLite, INSERT OR REPLACE fires delete triggers only if recursive triggers are enabled.

A column whose value the database computes from other columns of the same row, for example country text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (prefs ->> 'country') STORED. A STORED generated column can then be indexed like a normal column; since PostgreSQL 18 the default kind is VIRTUAL, computed when read.
A table that exists only for the current session (or transaction) and is dropped automatically afterwards. Use one to keep an intermediate result across several statements.

A hidden column PostgreSQL keeps on a row for internal bookkeeping. xmax records deletion or lock information for a row version; interpreting it as an inserted-versus-updated flag relies on implementation details.
The tree of steps a database will follow to run a query, such as scans, joins, sorts and aggregates. EXPLAIN shows it.

A PostgreSQL plan representation for a subquery that remains separate from the join tree. A correlated plain SubPlan can execute repeatedly; an uncorrelated hashed SubPlan builds a reusable hash table, and some uncorrelated expressions use an InitPlan.
A join method that builds a hash table of one input on the join key, then streams the other input and looks each row up. It suits large unsorted inputs joined on equality.
A plan node that groups or removes duplicate rows using a hash table. PostgreSQL can partition and spill hash aggregation to temporary files when its memory budget is exceeded.
A join method that, for each row of the outer input, scans or index-probes the inner input for matches. It is cheap when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index.
A join method that sorts both inputs on the join key (or reads them in order from indexes) and walks them together.

A PostgreSQL setting providing a base memory allowance for each sort or hash operation before temporary-file spilling. In PostgreSQL 16–18 its default is displayed as 4MB; a hash table’s allowance is generally this setting multiplied by hash_mem_multiplier, whose default is 2.0. Multiple operations, parallel workers and concurrent queries can consume many times the base allowance.
A PostgreSQL setting (from version 13) that lets hash-based operations use this many times work_mem; the default is 2.0 since version 15 (1.0 in versions 13 and 14).
example: With defaults, a hash table may use 4 MB × 2.0 = 8 MB.

definition: Writing part of a sort or hash operation to temporary files when its working data exceeds the memory budget, then reading it back. This adds I/O and can increase runtime; some structures, including PostgreSQL hashed SubPlans, cannot spill this way.
Reading rows by searching an index for the wanted keys and fetching only the matching rows, instead of reading the whole table.
example: WHERE id = 104 on the primary key reads a few pages instead of all of orders.

definition: Summaries PostgreSQL keeps about each column (common values, distribution, NULL fraction) and uses to estimate how many rows a condition will match. An expression such as prefs ->> 'country' has none unless indexed or given extended statistics.
The fraction of rows a condition keeps. The planner estimates it to choose plans: a selective filter (few rows) favours an index; an unselective one favours a full scan.
example: If 2 % of users have country = 'GB', that condition's selectivity is 0.02.

definition: How strongly a database separates concurrent transactions. PostgreSQL's default, READ COMMITTED, lets each statement see data committed before it started; SERIALIZABLE makes transactions behave as if run one at a time, failing some so they can be retried.
An error PostgreSQL raises at REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE isolation when a transaction cannot be ordered consistently with concurrent ones. The application should retry the transaction.
Several transactions or sessions running at overlapping times. Without care, two of them can both read "no row" and both insert, which is why upserts rely on unique indexes.

PostgreSQL’s decomposed JSON type. It does not preserve input whitespace, object key order or duplicate object keys, and it supports GIN indexes and containment operators; SQLite JSONB is a different, incompatible binary format.
example: The text {"b":2,"a":1,"a":3} is stored as {"a": 3, "b": 2}.

definition: A table column holding JSON documents, represented by a native JSON type, text or an engine-specific binary value. PostgreSQL json preserves the validated input text; jsonb stores a decomposed form. SQLite TEXT columns need an additional check when valid JSON must be enforced.
Data with some structure that varies from record to record, such as JSON documents whose keys differ between rows.
example: Event payloads where only cart events have a qty key are semi-structured.

definition: The body of data carried by a message or event, as opposed to its metadata. Here it is the JSON document stored for each event.

Operators that extract part of a JSON value. In PostgreSQL, -> returns json or jsonb and ->> returns text; #>> follows a path and returns text. In SQLite, -> returns JSON text and ->> returns a native SQL value.
example: In PostgreSQL payload ->> 'qty' returns the text '2', not the number 2.

definition: An expression that points into a JSON document, such as '$.device.os' in SQLite or the jsonpath language in PostgreSQL.
example: '$.device.os' selects the os key inside the device object.

definition: For PostgreSQL jsonb, @> tests whether the left JSON value contains the right according to JSON containment rules. Objects require matching keys and contained values; arrays have special rules that ignore element order and duplicate occurrences. A suitable GIN index can support the predicate.
example: payload @> '{"type":"cart"}' matches events 2 and 4.

definition: The jsonb operators ? (has this top-level key), ?| (has any of these keys) and ?& (has all of them). The default GIN operator class supports them.
example: payload ? 'tags' is true only for event 3.

definition: SQLite table-valued function that expands a JSON array into element rows or an object into member rows. PostgreSQL’s related jsonb_array_elements functions require arrays, so they are not interchangeable on arbitrary document shapes.
example: Event 3's tags array ["sale","new"] becomes two rows.

definition: Functions that build JSON from rows: json_group_array (SQLite) and jsonb_agg (PostgreSQL) collect values from many rows into a JSON array; json_object and jsonb_build_object build an object from key/value pairs.
example: json_group_array(o.id ORDER BY o.id) for Ana gives [101,103,107] on SQLite 3.44+; without aggregate ORDER BY, element order is unspecified.

definition: Functions that return a copy of a JSON document with a value inserted or replaced at a path: json_set in SQLite, jsonb_set in PostgreSQL.

Generalized Inverted Index: a PostgreSQL index type that indexes the elements inside a value (keys and values of a jsonb document, words in text, items in an array), so it can find rows containing a given element.
example: CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload) makes eligible containment predicates such as payload @> '{"type":"cart"}' available to the planner; a scan can still be cheaper.

definition: The rules connecting an index to supported operators. For a PostgreSQL jsonb GIN index, jsonb_ops supports containment, key existence and JSON path matching; jsonb_path_ops supports containment and JSON path matching but not key existence, with different size and selectivity trade-offs.

An index storing the result of an expression, such as an extracted JSON key. A predicate must use an expression the planner recognises as matching the indexed expression; index eligibility does not guarantee the planner will choose it.
example: CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload ->> 'type'));

definition: Checking a digital signature against the representation that was signed. Webhook schemes that sign raw request bytes require the original body: changing whitespace or key order can invalidate the signature, so preserving database JSON text alone is not a general raw-byte guarantee.

An INSERT clause that handles specified uniqueness conflicts by updating the existing row or skipping the proposed insert. PostgreSQL DO UPDATE requires a matching eligible non-deferrable unique constraint or index; exclusion constraints cannot arbitrate DO UPDATE.
Inside ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, the special table name excluded refers to the row that was proposed for insertion, while the table's own name refers to the existing row.
example: SET qty = stock.qty + excluded.qty adds the incoming quantity to the stored one.

definition: An operation whose effects occur as a whole or not at all. Atomicity alone does not promise every form of isolation; PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT also uses a unique index to resolve a conflicting concurrent insert.
example: ON CONFLICT makes "check for the key, then write" one atomic step.

definition: An SQLite conflict-resolution form (MySQL has REPLACE): on a uniqueness conflict it deletes the old row and inserts the new one, so unspecified columns fall back to their defaults. INSERT OR IGNORE instead skips the new row.
example: Replacing (4, 3, warehouse) with (4, 8) leaves (4, 8, NULL).

definition: The SQL-standard statement (PostgreSQL 15+) that joins a source to a target table and runs a different action for matched and unmatched rows: UPDATE, DELETE or INSERT. Unlike ON CONFLICT it can still hit a unique violation under concurrent inserts.

Loading or processing many rows together. A PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command may not affect the same target row twice; combine repeated input keys when they would violate that rule. DO NOTHING can instead skip repeated keys.
A unit of data size. In PostgreSQL settings 1 MB means 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes; elsewhere MB often means 1,000,000 bytes.
example: work_mem = 4MB lets one sort use about 4.2 million bytes.

definition: Describes an operation that has the same effect whether it runs once or several times. Setting qty to 15 is idempotent; adding 5 to qty is not, so replaying an additive upsert after a retry double-counts unless requests are de-duplicated.
example: Running UPDATE stock SET qty = 15 WHERE product_id = 1 twice still leaves 15; running qty = qty + 5 twice adds 10.

definition: An HTTP request that one service sends to a URL you register, to notify you of an event, usually with a JSON body. Receivers often store the raw JSON payload, which is one reason to keep JSON columns.
example: A payment provider POSTs a JSON document to your /webhooks/payments endpoint when a payment succeeds.

definition: A PostgreSQL 14+ recursive-CTE clause that computes a depth-first or breadth-first sort key. It does not control physical visitation order; apply ORDER BY to its generated key to order the output.
A window function returning the fraction of partition rows that sort before or are peers of the current row. All peers share a value, and the last peer group has value one.
A PostgreSQL plan for an uncorrelated subquery whose result can be computed once for a query execution and reused, such as a scalar aggregate independent of the outer row.
A window-frame boundary relative to the row being evaluated. In ROWS it means that row position; in RANGE or GROUPS it reaches the appropriate edge of its equal-ordering peer group.
A PostgreSQL value containing an ordered collection of elements of one SQL type. An integer array can record visited ids during a recursive traversal; it is distinct from a JSON array.
A month on the calendar rather than a fixed duration. Month arithmetic depends on date rules and month length; generating first-of-month dates avoids ambiguous month-end stepping.
The order of rows delivered to an aggregate. JSON and string aggregates can return different sequences for different input orders; an ORDER BY inside the aggregate specifies the required order.
A PostgreSQL object that generates successive numeric values, often used for identifiers. Obtaining a value is not rolled back, so conflicts and failed inserts can leave gaps.

A window function assigning an ordered position within a partition. ROW_NUMBER distinguishes rows, while RANK and DENSE_RANK give equal ordering peers equal ranks and differ in whether later ranks have gaps.
A PostgreSQL formatting function. With a date or timestamp and the pattern YYYY-MM, it produces a year-and-month text label suitable for a report.
A function rounding a number to a requested number of decimal places. PostgreSQL’s two-argument form requires numeric input; SQLite accepts its numeric values and returns a floating-point result.

An SQLite function checking whether its argument is valid JSON under selected format flags. A TEXT column does not itself validate a JSON document; a CHECK constraint using this function can reject malformed input.
A value written directly in SQL source, such as a numeric constant or quoted text. It is distinct from an identifier naming a table or column.

A constraint whose checking cannot be postponed until transaction commit. PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot use a deferrable uniqueness constraint as its arbiter, even when that constraint is currently checked immediately.
